intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: Seven austral summers of drilling and deployment; last string on 18 December 2010.
intervals.quote: Dedicated teams melted 60-centimeter diameter holes to a depth of 2,450 meters, deployed sensors, and commissioned strings from November to February each year from 2004 until 2011.

intervals.label: full-array operation
intervals.quote: Though IceCube had been taking data since 2005, it didn’t begin full operations until May 13, 2011, when the detector took its first set of data as a completed instrument.

name: IceCube in-ice array
notes: About 5,500 sensors were deployed in total including spares and IceTop; “fewer than 100 of the approximately 5,500 sensors are currently nonoperational” (official Detector page).
Derived fields (facility_id, document_ids) are not written; placement carries the site.

placements.note: Strings deployed from the 2004 season; full array since 18 December 2010.
placements.quote: IceCube, the South Pole neutrino observatory, is a cubic-kilometer particle detector made of Antarctic ice and located near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.

depth_max.quote: DOMs are attached to the cables beginning at a depth of 1,450 meter and ending at a depth of 2,450 meters.

depth_min.quote: DOMs are attached to the cables beginning at a depth of 1,450 meter and ending at a depth of 2,450 meters.

energy_range.note: Only the DeepCore threshold (~10 GeV) is stated numerically on the official page; the upper reach is given qualitatively as the PeV scale and above.
energy_range.quote: This denser configuration forms the DeepCore subdetector, which lowers the neutrino energy threshold to about 10 GeV, creating the opportunity to study neutrino oscillations.
energy_range.value: Roughly 100 GeV to the PeV scale and above in the main array; about 10 GeV with the DeepCore infill

instrumented_volume.quote: The IceCube detector is one cubic kilometer of ice—that would be enough water to fill one million swimming pools.

sensor_count.quote: The in-ice component of IceCube consists of 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs), each with a ten-inch photomultiplier tube and associated electronics.

string_count.quote: The DOMs are attached to vertical “strings,” frozen into 86 boreholes and arrayed over a cubic kilometer from 1,450 meters to 2,450 meters depth.

description.quote: The in-ice component of IceCube consists of 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs), each with a ten-inch photomultiplier tube and associated electronics.
description.value: Pressure sphere holding a ten-inch photomultiplier tube with on-board digitisation electronics

description.quote: The strings are deployed on a hexagonal grid with 125 meters spacing and hold 60 DOMs each. The vertical separation of the DOMs is 17 meters.
description.value: 86 strings on a hexagonal grid with 125 m horizontal spacing, 60 DOMs each, 17 m vertical separation

description.quote: This information is sent to computers in the IceCube Lab on the surface, which converts the messages from individual DOMs into light patterns that reveal the direction and energy of muons and neutrinos.
description.value: Surface building that receives, digitises and time-stamps the DOM data

summary.plain: The main part of IceCube: 86 cables lowered into holes melted in the ice, each carrying 60 basketball-sized light sensors that watch a cubic kilometre of ice for neutrino flashes.
summary.technical: Cubic-kilometre in-ice Cherenkov array: 5,160 DOMs on 86 strings between 1,450 m and 2,450 m depth, 125 m string spacing on a hexagonal grid, 17 m DOM spacing; ~98% of deployed DOMs operational and ~99% detector uptime (JINST 12 P03012).

technology.quote: The in-ice component of IceCube consists of 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs), each with a ten-inch photomultiplier tube and associated electronics.
technology.value: In-ice Cherenkov array of digital optical modules frozen into the Antarctic ice sheet
